query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a trace amount of boron (approximately 0.1 at.%) to a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy will induce the formation of intergranular boride precipitates, thereby improving elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to the same alloy without the boron addition.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy synthesized via powder metallurgy with a near-equimolar composition among the principal elements (including Ti and Ni) without any minor boron addition.
generation.intervention: Introduce 0.1 at.% boron into the alloy during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Heat treatment at elevated temperatures (around 1000 °C) for long durations (up to 1000 hours) in an inert (argon) atmosphere to simulate operating conditions in extreme environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of fine intergranular boride precipitates (e.g., titanium boride or nickel boride phases) that locally reinforce grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Boron segregates to the grain boundaries during processing and subsequent heat treatment and reacts with titanium or nickel to form stable boride phases, which improve grain boundary cohesion and inhibit grain boundary sliding or coarsening under prolonged high-temperature exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy with boron will exhibit higher microhardness and maintained grain-size stability at elevated temperatures compared to the control alloy without boron, leading to an overall enhancement in high-temperature mechanical strength.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties (e.g., microhardness and grain boundary integrity) measured in the titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without any boron addition under identical processing and testing conditions.
generation.boundary: The expected improvement is contingent on maintaining a low boron level (~0.1 at.%) in alloys with titanium and nickel as primary constituents; effects outside this composition range or with significantly higher boron levels have not been verified.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise nature and stability of the boride phases forming in a titanium- and nickel-primary HEA environment, and whether the minor boron addition will yield the same enhancement observed in other refractory HEAs given variations in processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy samples using identical powder metallurgy processes – one set with 0.1 at.% boron addition and one set without boron. Subject both sets to a heat treatment at approximately 1000 °C for 1000 hours in an argon atmosphere. Afterwards, evaluate the microstructural changes and mechanical properties.
measurements: Vickers microhardness of the alloy matrix and grain boundaries
Grain size and distribution of precipitated boride phases via scanning/transmission electron microscopy
Tensile strength and ductility assessments at elevated temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not show statistically significant improvements (e.g., at least a 5–10% increase in microhardness and enhanced indicators of grain boundary cohesion) compared to the control samples after prolonged heat treatment, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
## Abstract
AbstractTo develop strong refractory high-entropy alloys for use at elevated temperatures as well as to overcome grain-boundary brittleness, an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was prepared, and a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%) was added into the alloy. The microstructures of the alloys were characterized, and their macro-to-microscale mechanical properties were measured. The microstructural observations indicated that the matrices of both the alloys were composed of a body-centered cubic solid-solution structure, and the added boron induced the precipitation of hexagonal close-packed borides (most likely the (Hf, Zr)B2) at the grain boundaries. The modulus and hardness of differently oriented grains were about equivalent, suggesting a diminished anisotropy, and many small slips occurred on multiple {110} planes. While the hardness of the matrix was not increased, the intergranular precipitation of the borides markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion, the work hardenability and ductility were effectively improved with the addition of boron.Keywords: refractory alloy, high-entropy alloy, boride, grain boundary, mec
